paragraphs: Our police captain, Mihail Makarovitch Makarov, a retired lieutenant-colonel, was a widower and an excellent man. He had come to us only three years before, but he had won general esteem, mainly because he “knew how to keep society together.” He never lacked visitors and couldn’t have done without them. Someone or other was always dining with him, and he never sat down to table without guests. He gave regular dinners too, on all sorts of occasions, sometimes very surprising ones. The food wasn’t _recherché_, but there was plenty of it. The fish pies were excellent, and the wine made up in quantity for what it lacked in quality.

The first room his guests entered was a well-fitted billiard room, with pictures of English racehorses in black frames on the walls, an essential decoration, as we all know, for a bachelor’s billiard room. There was card playing at his house every evening, if only at one table. But often the whole society of our town, mammas and young ladies included, gathered there to dance. Mihail Makarovitch was a widower, but he didn’t live alone. His widowed daughter lived with him, together with her two unmarried daughters, grown girls who had finished their schooling. They were pleasant to look at and lively, and although everyone knew they would have no dowry, they drew all the fashionable young men to their grandfather’s house.

Mihail Makarovitch was by no means very capable at his work, though he did his duties no worse than many others. To speak plainly, he was a man of rather little education. He couldn’t always be relied on to understand the limits of his administrative power. It wasn’t so much that he failed to grasp certain reforms of the present reign, as that he made glaring blunders in interpreting them. This came not from any particular lack of intelligence but from carelessness, since he was always in too much of a hurry to go into the subject.

“I have the heart of a soldier rather than a civilian,” he used to say of himself. He had never even formed a clear idea of the basic principles of the reforms connected with the emancipation of the serfs. He only picked them up, so to speak, from year to year, adding to his knowledge without meaning to, through practice. And yet he was himself a landowner. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain that he would meet some of Mihail Makarovitch’s visitors there that evening, but he didn’t know which. As it happened, at that moment the prosecutor was playing whist at the police captain’s, together with Varvinsky, our district doctor, a young man who had only just come to us from Petersburg after taking a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor (he was really the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor), was a rather peculiar man of about thirty-five, inclined to be consumptive, and married to a fat, childless woman. He was vain and irritable, though he had a good mind and even a kind heart. It seemed that the only thing wrong with him was that he thought better of himself than his abilities warranted. That made him seem constantly uneasy. He had, besides, certain higher, even artistic, leanings, toward psychology, for instance, a special study of the human heart, a special knowledge of the criminal and his crime. He nursed a grievance on this score, considering that he had been passed over in the service, and being firmly convinced that in higher circles he had not been properly appreciated and had enemies. In gloomy moments he even threatened to give up his post and practice as a barrister in criminal cases. The unexpected Karamazov case stirred him deeply: “It was a case that might well be talked about all over Russia.” But I am getting ahead of myself.

Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov, the young investigating lawyer, who had come from Petersburg only two months before, was sitting in the next room with the young ladies. People talked about it afterwards and wondered that all these gentlemen should, as if on purpose, have been gathered together on the evening of “the crime” at the house of the chief authority. Yet it was perfectly simple and happened quite naturally.

Ippolit Kirillovitch’s wife had had a toothache for the last two days, and he had to go out to escape her groans. The doctor, by his very nature, couldn’t spend an evening anywhere but at cards. Nikolay Parfenovitch Nelyudov had been planning for three days to drop in at Mihail Makarovitch’s that evening, casually, so to speak, so as to startle the eldest granddaughter, Olga Mihailovna, slyly, by showing that he knew her secret: that he knew it was her birthday, and that she was deliberately trying to hide it so as not to have to give a dance. He expected a great deal of merriment, many playful jokes about her age and her fear of revealing it, about his knowing her secret and telling everybody, and so on. The charming young man was a great hand at such teasing. The ladies had nicknamed him “the naughty man,” and he seemed delighted with the name. He was extremely well-bred, however, of good family, education and feelings, and though he led a life of pleasure, his sallies were always innocent and in good taste. He was short and delicate-looking. On his white, slender, little fingers he always wore a number of big, glittering rings. When he was engaged in his official duties, he always became extraordinarily grave, as though he realized his position and the sacredness of the obligations laid upon him. He had a special gift for mystifying murderers and other criminals of the peasant class during questioning, and if he didn’t win their respect, he certainly succeeded in arousing their wonder.

Pyotr Ilyitch was simply dumbfounded when he went into the police captain’s house. He saw at once that everyone knew. They had actually thrown down their cards, and everyone was standing up and talking. Even Nikolay Parfenovitch had left the young ladies and run in, looking intense and ready for action. Pyotr Ilyitch was met with the astounding news that old Fyodor Pavlovitch really had been murdered that evening in his own house, murdered and robbed. The news had reached them only a moment before, in the following way.

Marfa Ignatyevna, the wife of old Grigory, who had been knocked senseless near the fence, was sleeping soundly in her bed and might well have slept till morning after the medicine she had taken. But all of a sudden she woke up, no doubt roused by a fearful epileptic scream from Smerdyakov, who was lying unconscious in the next room. That scream always came before his fits, and it always terrified and upset Marfa Ignatyevna. She could never get used to it. She jumped up and ran, half awake, to Smerdyakov’s room. But it was dark there, and she could only hear the sick man beginning to gasp and struggle. Then Marfa Ignatyevna herself screamed and was about to call her husband, but suddenly realized that when she got up, he hadn’t been beside her in bed. She ran back to the bed and began groping with her hands, but the bed really was empty. So he must have gone out—but where? She ran to the steps and called him timidly. She got no answer, of course, but she caught the sound of groans far away in the garden, in the darkness. She listened. The groans came again, and it was clear they came from the garden.
“Good Lord! Just as it was with Lizaveta Smerdyastchaya!” she thought distractedly. She went timidly down the steps and saw that the gate into the garden was open.
“He must be out there, poor dear,” she thought. She went up to the gate, and all at once she distinctly heard Grigory calling her by name, “Marfa! Marfa!” in a weak, moaning, dreadful voice.

“Lord, keep us from harm!” Marfa Ignatyevna murmured, and ran toward the voice, and that was how she found Grigory. But she found him not by the fence where he had been knocked down, but about twenty paces away. It came out later that he had crawled off when he came to himself, and had probably been a long time getting so far, losing consciousness several times. She saw at once that he was covered with blood, and she screamed at the top of her voice. Grigory was muttering incoherently:
“He has murdered ... his father murdered.... Why scream, silly ... run ... fetch someone....”

But Marfa went on screaming. Seeing that her master’s window was open and that a candle was burning in it, she ran there and began calling Fyodor Pavlovitch. But when she peeped in at the window, she saw a fearful sight. Her master was lying on his back on the floor, motionless. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked with blood. The candle on the table lit up brightly the blood and the motionless dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch. Terror-stricken, Marfa rushed away from the window, ran out of the garden, drew the bolt of the big gate and ran headlong by the back way to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Mother and daughter were both asleep, but they woke at Marfa’s desperate and persistent screaming and knocking at the shutter. Marfa, shrieking and screaming incoherently, managed to tell them the main fact and to beg for help. It happened that Foma had come back from his wanderings and was staying the night with them. They got him up at once, and all three ran to the scene of the crime. On the way, Marya Kondratyevna remembered that at about eight o’clock she had heard a dreadful scream from their garden. This was no doubt Grigory’s scream, “Parricide!” uttered when he caught hold of Mitya’s leg.

“One person screamed out and then was silent,” Marya Kondratyevna explained as she ran. They ran to the place where Grigory lay, and the two women, with Foma’s help, carried him to the lodge. They lit a candle and saw that Smerdyakov was no better, that he was writhing in convulsions, his eyes fixed in a squint, and that foam was running from his lips. They moistened Grigory’s forehead with water mixed with vinegar, and the water revived him at once. He asked immediately:
“Is the master murdered?”

Then Foma and both women ran to the house, and this time they saw that not only the window but also the door into the garden was wide open, though Fyodor Pavlovitch had locked himself in every night for the last week and hadn’t let even Grigory in on any pretext. Seeing that door open, they were afraid to go in to Fyodor Pavlovitch “for fear something should happen afterwards.” And when they went back to Grigory, the old man told them to go straight to the police captain. Marya Kondratyevna ran there and raised the alarm among the whole party at the police captain’s. She arrived only five minutes before Pyotr Ilyitch. So his story came not as his own guess and theory, but as direct confirmation, by a witness, of the theory everyone held about who the criminal was (a theory he had, in the bottom of his heart, refused to believe until that moment).

It was resolved to act with energy. The deputy police inspector of the town was ordered to take four witnesses, enter Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house and open an inquiry there on the spot, according to the regular forms, which I will not go into here. The district doctor, a zealous man, new to his work, almost insisted on going along with the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer.

I will note briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found quite dead, with his skull battered in. But with what? Most likely with the same weapon that had been used on Grigory. And as soon as that weapon was found, Grigory, who was at once given every possible medical help, described in a weak and breaking voice how he had been knocked down. They began searching with a lantern by the fence and found the brass pestle dropped in a most conspicuous place on the garden path. There were no signs of disturbance in the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch was lying. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up from the floor a big, thick envelope with the inscription: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” Below it Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, “For my little chicken.” There were three seals of red sealing wax on the envelope, but it had been torn open and was empty: the money was gone. They also found on the floor a piece of narrow pink ribbon, with which the envelope had been tied.

One piece of Pyotr Ilyitch’s evidence made a great impression on the prosecutor and the investigating magistrate: his idea that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would shoot himself before daybreak. He had resolved to do so, had spoken of it to Ilyitch, had taken the pistols, loaded them in front of him, written a letter, put it in his pocket, and so on. When Pyotr Ilyitch, though still unwilling to believe it, threatened to tell someone so as to prevent the suicide, Mitya had answered, grinning: “You’ll be too late.” So they had to hurry to Mokroe to find the criminal before he really did shoot himself.
“That’s clear, that’s clear!” the prosecutor repeated in great excitement. “That’s just the way with mad fellows like that: ‘I’ll kill myself tomorrow, so I’ll make merry till I die!’”
The story of how Mitya had bought the wine and provisions excited the prosecutor more than ever.

“Do you remember the fellow who murdered a merchant called Olsufyev, gentlemen? He stole fifteen hundred, went straight off to have his hair curled, and then, without even hiding the money, carrying it almost in his hand like that, he went off to the girls.”

All of them were delayed, however, by the inquiry, the search and the formalities in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. It all took time, and so, two hours before setting out, they sent on ahead to Mokroe the officer of the rural police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who had arrived in the town the morning before to collect his pay. He was instructed to avoid raising the alarm when he reached Mokroe, but to keep constant watch over the “criminal” until the proper authorities arrived, and also to get witnesses for the arrest, police constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did as he was told, kept his identity secret, and gave no one but his old acquaintance, Trifon Borissovitch, the slightest hint of his secret business. He had spoken to him just before Mitya met the landlord on the balcony, looking for him in the dark, and he noticed at once a change in Trifon Borissovitch’s face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew that he was being watched. The box with the pistols had been carried off by Trifon Borissovitch and put in a suitable place. Only after four o’clock, almost at sunrise, did all the officials, the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer, drive up in two carriages, each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s to do a post-mortem on the body the next day. But he was particularly interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

“Such violent and prolonged epileptic fits, recurring continually for twenty-four hours, are rarely met with, and they are of interest to science,” he declared enthusiastically to his companions, and as they left, they laughingly congratulated him on his find. The prosecutor and the investigating lawyer distinctly remembered the doctor saying that Smerdyakov couldn’t outlive the night.
After these long but, I think, necessary explanations, we will return to the moment in our tale at which we broke off.
